title: Cerebrospinal Fluid Shunt and Drain Infections

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man presented with a fever of 39°C and disorientation. He had a history of myelomeningocele and a ventriculoperitoneal shunt. He had no drug allergies. Investigations: Head CT scan: consistent with ventriculitis CSF microscopy: 250 nucleated cells with 85% neutrophils CSF glucose 25 mg/dL CSF protein 110 mg/dL CSF culture positive for Proteus mirabilis, sensitivities consistent with extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) production
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Meropenem While cefotetan, a cephamycin, is active against many ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae, it is not established for central nervous system infections and is vulnerable to treatment-emergent resistance with these strains. Ceftriaxone is not considered reliably active against ESBL-producing organisms. Gentamicin IV poorly penetrates the central nervous system and is not appropriate for monotherapy of central nervous system infections. Imipenem is reliably active against most ESBL-producing strains but is relatively inactive against Proteus mirabilis and should be avoided for treatment of serious infections caused by this organism. Imipenem is also widely believed to be the most epileptogenic carbapenem, which could be a concern in this case. Meropenem is active against ESBL-producing strains and is clinically established for treatment of central nervous system infections.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q4

questions.question: 45yo M with concerns for VP shunt infection.

parts.text: Give 4 clinical manifestations of VP shunt infection
Give 4 ways that VP shunts can become infected
Give two empiric antibiotic regimens
Give two most common pathogens
What is one other management strategy

questions.model_answer:
a) 4 clinical manifestations: fever, headache, nausea/vomiting, altered mental status/irritability (signs of shunt malfunction/increased ICP, meningismus, and abdominal pain/peritonitis with distal catheter infection are also acceptable).
b) 4 mechanisms of infection: (1) intraoperative contamination at the time of shunt placement (most common); (2) retrograde ascending infection from the distal catheter site (e.g., peritonitis with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt); (3) hematogenous seeding from a distant bacteremia; (4) erosion/breakdown of overlying skin with local wound contamination.
c) 2 empiric antibiotic regimens: (1) vancomycin + ceftazidime (or cefepime) for broad gram-positive plus antipseudomonal gram-negative coverage; (2) vancomycin + meropenem.
d) 2 most common pathogens: coagulase-negative staphylococci (S. epidermidis) and Staphylococcus aureus.
e) Other management strategy: surgical removal (externalization) of the entire shunt hardware with placement of a temporary external ventricular drain, in addition to antibiotics.

questions.question: 3 yo child who had a VP shunt put in 1 year ago.

parts.text: Give 4 clinical manifestations of VP shunt infection
Give 4 mechanisms of how VP shunts can become infected
Give two most common pathogens
Give two empiric antibiotic regimens
What is one other management strategy

questions.model_answer:
a) 4 clinical manifestations: fever, headache/irritability, vomiting, altered mental status or signs of shunt malfunction (increased ICP); abdominal pain/peritonitis if distal catheter infected.
b) 4 mechanisms: (1) intraoperative contamination at placement; (2) retrograde infection from the distal (peritoneal) catheter; (3) hematogenous seeding; (4) skin erosion/wound breakdown with local contamination.
c) 2 most common pathogens: coagulase-negative staphylococci (S. epidermidis) and Staphylococcus aureus.
d) 2 empiric antibiotic regimens: (1) vancomycin + ceftazidime (or cefepime); (2) vancomycin + meropenem.
e) Other management strategy: surgical shunt removal/externalization with temporary external ventricular drainage alongside antibiotics.

questions.question: VP shunt infection.

parts.text: What are the two most common organisms?
Name 4 manifestation of shunt infection?
Name 4 mechanisms of shunt infection?
Name 2 treatment regimens?
What adjunctive measure is recommended for treatment in addition to antibiotics?

questions.model_answer:
a) 2 most common organisms: coagulase-negative staphylococci (S. epidermidis) and Staphylococcus aureus.
b) 4 manifestations: fever, headache, vomiting, altered mental status/signs of shunt malfunction (or abdominal pain/peritonitis if distal catheter involved).
c) 4 mechanisms: intraoperative contamination, retrograde infection from the distal catheter, hematogenous seeding, skin erosion/wound breakdown.
d) 2 treatment regimens: (1) vancomycin + ceftazidime (or cefepime); (2) vancomycin + meropenem.
e) Adjunctive measure: complete surgical removal of the shunt hardware with temporary external ventricular drainage in addition to antibiotics.

questions.question: VP shunt infection

parts.text: What are 4 symptoms
What are 4 ways this infection can develop?
What are 2 MOST COMMON organisms
What are 2 empiric treatment regimens?
What must you do to ensure the infection is treated?

questions.model_answer:
a) 4 symptoms: fever, headache, vomiting, altered mental status/signs of increased ICP (or abdominal pain/peritonitis with distal catheter infection).
b) 4 ways infection develops: intraoperative contamination at placement, retrograde ascending infection from the distal catheter, hematogenous seeding, skin erosion/wound breakdown with local contamination.
c) 2 most common organisms: coagulase-negative staphylococci (S. epidermidis) and Staphylococcus aureus.
d) 2 empiric treatment regimens: (1) vancomycin + ceftazidime (or cefepime); (2) vancomycin + meropenem.
e) To ensure the infection is treated: surgically remove the entire shunt hardware and place a temporary external ventricular drain, alongside systemic antibiotics (device removal is essential - antibiotics alone are usually inadequate due to biofilm).

questions.question: A patient has a VP shunt infection.

parts.text: What are 3 symptoms suggestive of shunt infection.
What are 4 sources/mechanisms of infection.
2 empiric choices for treatment.
2 most likely pathogens.

cohort_answer.text: Symptoms: can be subtle (common pathogens CoNS/C. acnes elicit minimal inflammation), onset may be insidious; headache, change in LOC, nausea, lethargy (often shunt malfunction with infection); fever (14-92%); pain at peritoneal/pleural ends; pain at proximal end (meningitis/ventriculitis). Mechanisms: retrograde infection from distal end via peritonitis (rare); via skin (direct access for sampling/drug infusion, skin breakdown over shunt or failure to heal); hematogenous seeding (especially ventriculoatrial shunts); colonization at time of surgery (MOST COMMON). Empiric: Ceftazidime/vancomycin, Meropenem/vancomycin, Cefepime/vancomycin (healthcare associated). Pathogens: CoNS (S. epidermidis) > S. aureus (staphylococci together 55-95%) > Enterobacteriaceae (6-20%) > Streptococci (8-10%) > diphtheroids (1-14%) > anaerobes (6%) > yeast.

questions.question: What are the typical organisms infecting in the following scenarios.

parts.text: Cochlear implants.
Laceration that occurs in a lake
Rat bite in a child who now has fever and rash
Guy competing in a triathlon in South America has fever, high LFTs and conjunctival suffusion

cohort_answer.text: Cochlear implants: meningitis most commonly S. pneumoniae, less often H. influenzae; localized wound infection most commonly S. aureus (also CoNS, streptococci, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Achromobacter xylosoxidans, Candida albicans); mastoiditis most commonly S. pneumoniae, S. pyogenes, S. aureus, Pseudomonas spp, H. influenzae. Lake laceration (fresh/brackish water): Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Aeromonas hydrophila, Chromobacterium violaceum (immunosuppression/CGD), Mycobacterium fortuitum, Plesiomonas shigelloides, Edwardsiella tarda, Burkholderia pseudomallei, Streptococcus iniae (fish preparation); salt water: Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae (fish preparation), Mycobacterium marinum, Shewanella spp, Vibrio vulnificus. Rat bite: Streptobacillus moniliformis (most US cases); Spirillum minus (Asia). Triathlon South America: Leptospirosis - abrupt fever, rigors, myalgias, headache after incubation 2-26 days (average 10); conjunctival suffusion important but often overlooked sign (~55% of patients), uncommon in other diseases; subconjunctival hemorrhages also occur.
